A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BESPOKE with the same authors, benchmark and evaluation framework. The main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluator–human agreement measurements, six-model personalization experiments, history-retrieval results and gold-information experiments in Section 4.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds evaluator-backbone, rubric-generator, explicit-preference and noisy-information experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, personalization evaluator, gold-claim recall calculation, profile construction and query-expansion procedures remain intact. Alternative evaluator backbones are tested within the existing framework. Newly specifying k=6 and clarifying prompts do not establish a changed proposed method.

E1.justification: The 30 users, 2,870 sessions, 150 queries and four task types remain unchanged. v2 adds explicit gold-information-need and controlled noisy-evidence scenarios, changing evaluation input conditions within the existing benchmark. Expanded descriptions of annotator backgrounds do not establish a broader sampled population.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-oss-120B and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 evaluator alternatives in Table 7 and compares Qwen-generated versus GPT-5-generated rubrics in Table 8. The six response-generation models, original evaluator baselines and retrieval comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols provide gold information needs directly to four models, replace 0%, 30%, 50% or 70% of gold information with unrelated content for the Sonar pair, and vary evaluator backbones and rubric generators independently. These substantially extend the experimental controls; the original Table 4 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's history-context, query-expansion and gold-information analyses, v2 tests evaluator generality across model families, sensitivity to the rubric generator, the gap between explicit preferences and history-based inference, and robustness to noisy evidence (Tables 6–9). The earlier qualitative case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports evaluator-validation point estimates without corresponding run counts or uncertainty. v2 reports three-run means and standard deviations in Table 3 and the new Tables 7–8, introducing uncertainty reporting for a central validation component. This does not establish that v1 used fewer repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 3's full-evaluator average Pearson/Spearman/feedback accuracy changes from 0.853/0.857/0.870 to 0.847/0.853/0.881 under newly reported three-run aggregation. Tables 6–9 add noise, evaluator, rubric and oracle results. Dataset averages are corrected from 73.48/24.34 to 71.77/23.90 search/chat sessions without changing individual user rows. Tables 4–5 retain their scores.

T1.justification: The task definitions, evaluator formulation, gold-claim recall formula and Shannon diversity equations are substantively unchanged. Renaming factual coverage as gold information coverage does not alter its mathematical definition. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a realistic human-grounded personalization benchmark, evaluation with diagnostic feedback, and systematic analyses of search-augmented personalization. The added experiments support these contributions without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the oracle experiment as identifying history-based preference inference as the primary bottleneck and qualifies reasoning models' advantage by showing sensitivity to noisy evidence. Appendix A adds proprietary-evaluator limitations, rubric self-consistency concerns and an instruction-following explanation for backbone differences. Recall is also framed more precisely as gold-information coverage.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands annotation documentation: cohort expertise and interests, compensation and withdrawal terms, privacy screening, annotation instructions, revision-based quality control, k=6, and construction/evaluation costs (Appendices B and C.5). It also provides a direct repository pointer. These are expanded disclosures rather than evidence that the retained dataset was reconstructed.

R1.justification: v2 adds MMLU-Pro, Humanity's Last Exam, IFEval and IFBench references to contextualize backbone capabilities, while removing earlier citations including VerifiNER, MT-RAIG and Panickssery et al. The principal positioning against existing personalization and search benchmarks in Section 2 and Table 1 remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted wording and terminology edits, makes task formulation an unnumbered paragraph, and presents personalization before coverage in the evaluation description. It removes the appendix contents page and adds acknowledgements and an LLM-use disclosure. Most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper with extensive figure and table reflow. Figure 2 rearranges evaluation components, Figure 4 changes from a two-by-two grid to vertically stacked plots, and Tables 6–9 are added. Table 3 incorporates uncertainty displays; existing appendix examples and prompts are largely reformatted and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's central evaluator validation through alternative evaluator backbones, an independent rubric generator and repeated-run uncertainty reporting, addressing v1's reliance on a single proprietary evaluator configuration. Oracle and noise controls improve diagnostic evidence, while annotation disclosures improve transparency. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix A.4 claims improvements across all criteria, although Gemini-2.5-Pro's oracle tone score is 80.53 versus 84.40 in Table 4. This limits that interpretation but does not outweigh the stronger validation.
